excerpt: There is a massive gap between claiming AI will boost productivity and actually fixing bottlenecks. Lessons from Canada's healthcare system and Humber River Hospital.
---
Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports."[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names sectors where AI will create "outsized value": healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because it's the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here's the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it "AI" but it's not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive without making a big difference. 

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

[^1]: Bank of Canada, [Time to Break the Glass: Fixing Canada's Productivity Problem](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/03/time-to-break-the-glass-fixing-canadas-productivity-problem/)
[^2]: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, [Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all)
[^3]: Humber River Hospital Foundation, [Humber River Hospital's Command Centre Has Created 23 Virtual Beds](https://www.hrhfoundation.ca/blog/humber-river-hospitals-command-centre-has-created-23-virtual-beds/)
[^4]: GE Healthcare, [Humber River Hospital Command Centre: One Year in Review](https://www.gehealthcare.com/content/dam/gehc/sitecore-migrated-assets/gehc/us/files/services/value-partnerships/20190121-humber-river-hospital-command-centre-one-year-in-review.pdf) (PDF)

[^5]: CBC News, [Medical AI transcriber for Ontario doctors 'hallucinated,' generated errors: auditor general](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/ai-scribe-system-hallucinations-9.7197049)
</context>

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. Determine Mode: New Post or Revision Ask the user whether they are: - **Creating a new post** → follow the New Post path (steps 2-4) - **Revising an existing post** → follow the Revision path (step 5) If the user references an existing post by name or slug, treat it as a revision. --- ## New Post Path ### 2. Gather Required Information Ask the user for: - **Title**: The blog post title - **Topic/Content**: What the post is about (can be an outline, draft, or description) - **Category**: Which category it belongs to (show available options) Available categories: - `agile-engineering-practices` - Engineering practices like TDD, CI/CD, refactoring - `anti-patterns` - Common mistakes and how to avoid them - `artificial-intelligence` - AI and its intersection with Agile - `books` - Book reviews and recommendations - `effective-scrum-and-core-agile` - Core Scrum and Agile concepts - `modern-leadership-and-organizational-change` - Leadership and change management - `product-ownership` - Product Owner topics and product management - `resilience-and-meaningful-metrics` - Metrics, measurement, and team health - `scrum-by-example` - Practical Scrum examples and case studies. For a new story in this series, paste the recurring cast from `.claude/templates/scrum-by-example-dramatis-personae.mdx` so characters stay consistent across posts. - `scrum-events-and-artifacts` - Sprint events, backlogs, etc. - `team-dynamics-and-people` - Team collaboration and interpersonal topics ### 3. Generate the Slug Create a URL-friendly slug from the title: - Convert to lowercase - Replace spaces with hyphens - Remove special characters - Keep it concise but descriptive Example: "GenAI vs Human Intelligence - a Reality Check" → `gen-ai-vs-human-intelligence-a-reality-check` ### 4. Create Directory and MDX File Create the blog post directory and file: ``` src/content/blog/{slug}/ ├── index.mdx └── images/ (if images are needed) ``` Use this template structure: ```mdx --- title: "{title}" date: "{YYYY-MM-DD}" draft: true categories: - "{category-slug}" coverImage: '@/content/blog/{slug}/images/{cover-image-name}.jpg' excerpt: '' --- import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro'; import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro'; import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro'; {content} ``` Then proceed to **Step 6: Internal Linking**. --- ## Revision Path ### 5. Audit the Existing Post Read the existing post and perform these checks: **5a. Check the content-work-plan for specific guidance:** Read the vault at `APR/Analytics/content-work-plan.md` and search for the post slug. The work plan may have specific instructions for this post (content changes, merge targets, linking maps). Follow those instructions if present. **5b. Linking audit — count what exists:** - How many **outbound blog post links** does it have? (Target: 2-3 minimum) - How many **inbound links** from other posts? Use `Grep` to search for the post slug across `src/content/blog/`. (Target: 2-3 minimum; if zero, this is an orphan) - Does it have a **course link**? (Add one only if topic naturally aligns) - Does it link to a **pillar page or cluster hub**? (Add if one exists for this cluster) - Do NOT count or flag glossary links — the auto-linker handles those at build time. **5c. Content quality check:** - Does the opening **name a specific pain point or problem**? Or does it start with a generic definition/history? (See Step 7: Content Framing) - Are there **outdated references**, broken links, or stale examples? - Could it benefit from a `` or `` for key takeaways? - Does it have meaningful **alt text** on all images? **5d. Frontmatter check:** - If making a substantive content update, add or update `lastUpdated: "YYYY-MM-DD"` in the frontmatter (not for mechanical changes like link fixes or quote conversions) - Does it have an `excerpt`? (Flag if missing, but do not AI-generate one) **5e. Report findings to the user:** Present a summary of what was found and recommend changes. Group into: - **Required** (orphan status, missing cluster links, content-work-plan instructions) - **Recommended** (framing improvements, outdated references, missing course link) Then proceed to **Step 6: Internal Linking** to address any gaps. --- ## Shared Steps (Both New and Revision) ### 6. Internal Linking (Performance-Informed) Every blog post must be woven into the site's content web. Internal linking directly improves search rankings (average position improved from 33.6 to 18.9 after clustering work began) and 42% of posts are orphans with zero inbound links. **In the post, include:** 1. **2-3 links to related existing blog posts.** Find posts in the same topic cluster (see the vault at `APR/Analytics/content-work-plan.md` Phase 2B for cluster definitions). Use `Grep` to search for related content. Contextual links woven into sentences are better than a list. 2. **Do NOT recommend manual glossary links in blog posts.** The build-time glossary auto-linker (`src/utils/glossaryLookup.ts`) handles this automatically for every term it knows about (up to 2 occurrences per term). Manual glossary links in blog posts duplicate the auto-linker's work and create maintenance drag. The only glossary-related gap worth flagging is a *missing alias* on a glossary entry that prevents the auto-linker from matching (bracketed titles like `'X [ABBR]'` and suffix-style titles like `'Wizard of Oz MVP'` need explicit aliases — see the `glossary-entry` skill). Manual glossary links are appropriate only *inside glossary entries themselves*, because glossary entries are not auto-linked. 3. **1 link to a pillar page or cluster hub** if one exists for this topic area. 4. **1 natural in-content course link** if the topic aligns with a course. Course pages sit outside the blog-to-blog graph, so a single course link does not dilute cluster density; it's safe to include where the topic genuinely connects. Course URLs: - CSM: `/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/` - CSPO: `/courses/certified-scrum-product-owner-cspo-training/` - A-CSM: `/courses/advanced-certified-scrummaster-acsm-training/` - CSD: `/courses/csd-developer-training/` - CSP-SM: (check current URL) **For revisions:** Only add links that are missing. Do not duplicate links the post already has. **Category-to-cluster mapping** (use to find related posts): | Category | Primary Cluster(s) | |----------|-------------------| | `resilience-and-meaningful-metrics` | Cluster 1: Metrics & Resilience | | `team-dynamics-and-people` | Cluster 2: Team Dynamics | | `product-ownership` | Cluster 3: Product Ownership | | `modern-leadership-and-organizational-change` | Cluster 4: Org Change | | `scrum-events-and-artifacts` | Cluster 5: Scrum Events | | `scrum-by-example`, `anti-patterns` | Cluster 6: ScrumMaster Role | | `agile-engineering-practices` | Cluster 7: Engineering Practices | | `effective-scrum-and-core-agile` | Cluster 8: Scrum Fundamentals | | `artificial-intelligence` | GenAI Cluster | ### 7. Content Framing (Performance-Informed) These patterns consistently outperform across social media, newsletters, and organic search: - **Name the pain.** Practical, problem-focused content outperforms abstract or generic content everywhere. "Sprint Planning from Hell" outperforms "Effective Scrum launches true teams." Frame the post around a specific problem the reader recognizes. - **Myth-busting resonates**, especially on Mastodon (the highest-quality traffic source at 6.7 min avg sessions, 30.7% bounce rate). Posts debunking common beliefs consistently get the highest engagement. - **Lead with a concrete scenario or pain point**, not a definition or history lesson. The top-performing newsletter had 26% CTR because it opened with a recognizable problem (tedious meetings) and offered actionable steps. - **Avoid pure announcements or abstract theory** without educational value. These have the highest newsletter unsubscribe rates (>1%). **For revisions:** If the existing post opens with a generic definition or abstract statement, suggest reframing the opening around a concrete problem. Do not rewrite without the user's approval. ### 8. I will focus on the health sector, because it's the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here's the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it "AI" but it's not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive without making a big difference. 

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports."[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names sectors where AI will create "outsized value": healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because it's the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here's the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it "AI" but it's not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive without making a big difference. 

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports."[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. I made [the same argument about the federal government](/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/): dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess.

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names sectors where AI will create "outsized value": healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because it's the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here's the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it "AI" but it's not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive without making a big difference. 

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

---
title: "Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity"
date: "2026-07-10"
draft: true
categories:
  - "artificial-intelligence"
excerpt: There is a massive gap between claiming AI will boost productivity and actually fixing bottlenecks. Lessons from Canada's healthcare system and Humber River Hospital.
---
Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. “Increase Canada’s business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports.”[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. I made [the same argument about the federal government](/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/): dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess.

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names sectors where AI will create "outsized value": healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because it's the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our [Systems Thinking](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here's the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it "AI" but it's not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive without making a big difference. 

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can [make an organization more fragile, not more resilient](/blog/is-ai-making-your-organization-fragile-or-more-resilient/).

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

16	The strategy names sectors where AI will create “outsized value”: healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?
17	
18	There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.
19	
20	## Healthcare
21	I will focus on the health sector, because it’s the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. 22	
23	Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 
24	
25	Putting on our [Systems Thinking](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) hat, we want to ask two questions:
26	- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
27	- Why are hospital beds so full?
28	
29	### Hospital beds
30	- Low population to hospital bed ratio
31	- Waiting lists for long term care
32	- Staffing shortages
33	
34	### Emergency Room Volume
35	- Lack of family doctor
36	- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
37	- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
38	- Seasonal flu et al
39	
40	None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 
41	
42	One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they’re paying attention[^3] to:
43	- Emergency Department volume
44	- Bed allocations and assignments
45	- Room cleaning
46	- Critical care capacity
47	- Surgical scheduling
48	- Discharge planning
49	
50	Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.
51	
52	GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn’t the central feature. 53	
54	AI is useful here, because they’ve studied the flow of the system. They’ve established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. 55	
56	The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can’t see.
57	
58	AI didn’t make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.
59	
60	### Family Doctors and GenAI
61	Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 
62	
63	After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

72

title: "Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity"
date: "2026-07-10"
categories:

excerpt: There is a massive gap between claiming AI will boost productivity and actually fixing bottlenecks. Lessons from Canada's healthcare system and Humber River Hospital.
---
Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. “Increase Canada’s business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports.”[^2] I’m reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. I made [the same argument about the federal government](/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/): dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess.

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names sectors where AI will create “outsized value”: healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because it’s the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn’t make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we’ve sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn’t make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation.

Putting on our [Systems Thinking](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go: walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system.

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they’re paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn’t the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they’ve studied the flow of the system. They’ve established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here’s the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it “AI” but it’s not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can’t see.

AI didn’t make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity.

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don’t cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) In an attempt to reduce the unpaid labour, many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive without making a big difference.

GenAI might help here, however we’ve solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn’t a magic wand and it isn’t a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can [make an organization more fragile, not more resilient](/blog/is-ai-making-your-organization-fragile-or-more-resilient/).

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can’t keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can’t expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds.

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

GenAI might help here, however we’ve solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

3	date: "2025-08-15"

10	excerpt: 'GenAI and PredictiveAI promise greater efficiency, but speeding up workers often makes bottlenecks worse. Focus on these three things instead.'
11	---
12	import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
13	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
14	import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';

16	
17	The Prime Minister of Canada told federal government to become more efficient and cut their budgets, and it's suggested that artificial intelligence can play a key role.[^1]
18	
19	I know AI, I have seen the inside workings of many government departments, and I know something about efficiency. All politics aside (no, really), I have concerns. Using AI isn't a bad idea, but it needs to be approached in a responsible way. *Especially* if you're the federal government. (For delivery teams working through the same questions, our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/) is an evidence-based, cohort-based course.)
20	
21	<CalloutBox>
22	*Oxford English Dictionary: **efficiency** (-shensi) n. State or quality of being efficient; (Mech. & Phys.) ratio of useful work done to total energy expended or heat taken in;*
23	
24	Be careful, a focus on efficiency can make systems worse. We save a few dollars, but slow down the whole system. "Do more with less" reduces quality and eventually costs more.
25	</CalloutBox>
26	
27	There are two major kinds of "AI" in use today. GenerativeAI and PredictiveAI. Generative AI is the tool most of us are familiar with (ChatGPT, Claude, etc). We write some text, and the model *generates* a response. PredictiveAI attempts to *predict* future events based on past data — for example, in an emergency department, deciding who needs hospital admission for pneumonia and who can recover at home.
28	
29	Can either of these tools help make the federal government more efficient?
30	- GenAI is excellent at creating a large body of text or other content quickly. GenAI promises that it will speed up many tasks, allowing each worker to get more stuff done.
31	- PredictiveAI makes many promises, including automating decision-making.
32	
33	Will either of these make departments more efficient? Assuming GenAI made everyone faster (it doesn't) and that it didn't make mistakes (it does), we expect GenAI to speed up departments magically so they can generate more "stuff". Lots of stuff makes it seem like people are busy. Busy might appear to be efficient, but those aren't synonymous.
34	
35	The problem is the bottlenecks. You know them from the daily commute, that place on the highway where it always slows down. The only place to improve is the bottleneck itself (see Theory of Constraints for more details). So even if GenAI does speed up individual workers, unless that person is the bottleneck, the most likely outcome is that it will make the logjam worse.
36	
37	<Figure
38	  src={aiBottleneck}
39	  alt="sketch of GenAI making stuff faster, but with a bottleneck"
40	  caption="sketch of GenAI making stuff faster, but with a bottleneck"
41	/>
42	
43	 Even if we magically fixed one bottleneck (example: issuing passports), there might be consequences (e.g. issuing emergency travel documents for Canadians stuck overseas). Without a clear set of priorities, we might make the whole system worse.
44	
45	I've seen inside many federal government departments, agencies, and crown corporations. I've seen departments where the work has already been approved. The work item should take 15-20 days of working time, and it spends 75-90 days waiting for additional management decision-making.  In this case, the bottleneck is the speed of decision-making and the lack of autonomy. All but the smallest decisions need to get approval from a senior manager; this is a side effect of a risk-averse culture. The manager demands more information to make each decision, so team members are pulled off their current work to find that information. The number of decisions managers are expected to make is overwhelming, so many vital decisions wait on their desks for weeks or months. If people use GenAI simply to create more quantity rather than quality, it will increase the number of decisions that managers need to make, snowballing the problem.
46	
47	If decisions are waiting for months, can we responsibly use PredictiveAI to speed the process? In theory, maybe. But in practice, PredictiveAI makes decisions based on past data, and that can lead to poor predictions when the training data was incomplete, or it was biased, or future conditions don't match the past. Even if PredictiveAI was good at making forecasts of what will happen in thousands of cases (it isn't), that predictive value is useless at making each single decision (e.g. Should we send this specific patient home?) In these cases, it's no better than flipping a coin.[^2]
48	
49	Finally, the focus on efficiency creates other problems. When everything is about efficiency, the focus is primarily on the cost of the work. Missing from the equation: are we doing the right job? Is the work being done well? Efficiency creates systems that are fragile, with many handoffs that are slower at delivering results.
50	
51	Over years of making mistakes, I've learned what does work:
52	- Define what results matter and have clear priorities. Most groups can sustain only three priorities, max, at one time. Overall priorities matter, so when there is a conflict it needs to be clear which item(s) must be finished first.
53	- Study the flow of the system. The easiest way is to build a Kanban board and see where work gets stuck or spends time waiting. Find the bottleneck and consider how to improve throughput there.
54	- Push decision-making down to people doing the work. Most decisions are reversible, and so are lower cost. Reversible choices can be made with less information and less authority... and, therefore, less delays.
55	
56	Can GenAI help? Perhaps once we've found the bottleneck. Some work can be sped up with GenAI but most valuable work still requires a thoughtful person. Instead of chasing magic promises, bottlenecks are most often solved by asking people to help out with the work.
57	
58	This isn't a one-time fix. No team or organization stays the same forever, and that is particularly true in government departments. For the best chance of success, they will need to keep measuring the flow and running experiments. Only then can they find opportunities to use GenAI to legitimately improve efficiency. 1	---
2	title: "Using GenAI to Code? Not So Fast"
3	date: "2025-07-23"
4	lastUpdated: '2025-07-23'
5	draft: false
6	categories:
7	  - "agile-engineering-practices"
8	  - "artificial-intelligence"
9	coverImage: '@/content/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/images/ai-promise-vs-reality.jpg'
10	excerpt: 'New research suggests AI coding tools may actually slow down experienced developers by 19%, despite developers perceiving they work 20% faster.'
11	---
12	import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
13	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
14	import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
15	import aiPromiseReality from '@/content/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/images/ai-promise-vs-reality.jpg'
16	
17	AI coding agents have been sold to us, making big promises of how much faster we will work using them. In our "[The Real Cost of AI-Generated Code: It's Not All It's Cracked Up To Be](/blog/the-real-cost-of-ai-generated-code-it-s-not-all-it-s-cracked-up-to-be/)" article, we showed that this speed is coming at a cost with increased Technical Debt and decreased maintainability. The Agile community has witnessed this many times over the years. (There is a longer-term cost too: [AI and Skill Atrophy](/glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/) erodes the very judgment we need to review the code the model wrote.)
18	
19	Aside from sharpening our skills, most things that promise to help us go faster come at cost. Now there is new research that calls into question even the speed-up of writing code with GenAI. Sorting hype from evidence is exactly what we do in our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/), a cohort-based course for development teams.
20	<CalloutBox heading="Read for Yourself and Decide">
21	[Summary](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/) and the full paper: [Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089).
22	
23	*Caveats: this is a single research paper which studied senior developers who contributed to open source projects. The codebases for the projects were large (over 1,000,000 lines of code), and the developers were familiar with their projects. Some effort was made to ensure that the projects had good-quality code in the first place. So the paper is studying a narrow slice of work, and the results might not generalize.*
24	</CalloutBox>
25	The researchers paid the participants to address outstanding issues in their projects. For each issue, they were told to use AI or **no**-AI. They were also asked to forecast how long the issue would take to fix. When allowed to use AI, the developers predicted they would go 25% faster than an unaided human. That's not what happened. The AI-enabled developers took, on average, 19% **longer** to complete the task. Interestingly, even though they were notably slower than their non-AI aided colleagues, they perceived that they had worked 20% faster.
26	
27	These results are contrary to what we see reported elsewhere.
28	- Some research has been done using either simple tasks like implementing a basic HTTP server[^1] or synthetic tasks[^2] - neither of which necessarily generalizes to the real world tasks.
29	- Other studies report on the number of lines of code generated **UGH!!**[^3], commits, or pull requests[^4]. Of course, none of this is correlated with high-quality code that meets the business needs.
30	- SWE and other benchmarks often make it seem like AI tools are good at solving a wide range of problems. However, these benchmarks have flaws. The only metric that matters to them is: Did the code pass the test? But the projects used for the benchmark have incomplete test cases. The generated code might fix the original issue but introduce a new bug. Worse, the code isn't examined to see if it is readable or fits the established patterns of the code base.
31	- Much of what we're seeing to support the value of GenAI tool is self-report data. As the above research study illustrates, the self-report data doesn't necessarily correspond to reality! As an example, I perceived my last bike ride was 20% faster than the previous one, but the data sadly shows it was merely average.
32	- DORA report (State of DevOps) - The DORA 2024 report[^5] has missed the boat, measuring developers' perceptions about AI. It found that they feel more productive and believe they have reduced complexity. But, as seen above, self-report data isn't the most reliable when it comes to performance.
33	
34	More caveats on the research paper:
35	- There is a risk that the paper's methodology missed something important about real work (although this paper already has a better methodology than previous papers).
36	- Many of the developers hadn't used Cursor before. Maybe with more practice they would have been faster.
37	- The study used senior developers. Maybe junior developers would gain more benefit from AI assistance. But then that leaves the question of how do junior developers grow and become senior? Will junior developers spend enough time reviewing the generated code, understand it, and verify that it's a good fit?
38	- This is a single paper. Maybe a larger sample size or a diffent mix of people might have found a different result.
39	
40	**What this paper does is give me pause in accepting the statements that claim AI is magically improving developer productivity.** For a concrete example of how AI coding tools struggle with real tasks, see the results of our [AI Code Generation and the Tennis Kata](/blog/ai-code-generation-and-the-tennis-kata/) experiment.
41	<Figure
42	  src={aiPromiseReality}
43	  alt="sketch of GenAI promises vs reality"
44	  caption="sketch of GenAI promises vs reality"
45	/>
46	What would I like to see? I would like papers to look at additional questions not covered in this study:
47	- Was the code change a sensible size? Generally, we don't want bug fixes to be large changes. When bug fixes are large, it introduces new risks.
48	- Did the AI generated code fit the idioms used in the project?
49	- Was the AI generated code readable?
50	- Did the AI avoid adding any new dependencies?
51	
52	It is early days in our use of GenAI and software development. The models themselves will likely improve (example: context windows), and tool vendors will find ways to improve their tools so the LLM has more information about the codebase. I also know of some developers who are using a BDD style of development coupled with code generation, which might well pay off.
53	
54	I hope we all learn to be more skeptical of promises about productivity increases without first examining the methodology underneath. (I, for one, have written off the DORA Reports as unreliable.) In our [Certified ScrumMaster workshops](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/), we focus on what actually helps teams deliver value, not promises of faster output.
55	
56	<LinkList heading = "Related Blog Entries">
57	- [AI-Generated Code Quality and the Challenges we all face](/blog/ai-generated-code-quality-problems/)
58	- [GenAI Code Quality: The Fundamental Flaws and How Bluffing Makes It Worse](/blog/genai-code-quality-fundamental-flaws-and-how-bluffing-makes-it-worse/)
59	- [GenAI vs Human Intelligence: A Reality Check](/blog/gen-ai-vs-human-intelligence-a-reality-check/)
60	</LinkList>
61	
62	[^1]: "The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot," https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590
63	[^2]: "Significant Productivity Gains through Programming with Large Language Models," https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3661145
64	[^3]: "Sea Change in Software Development: Economic and Productivity Analysis of the AI-Powered Developer Lifecycle," https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15033
65	[^4]: "The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers," https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4945566
66	[^5]: "DORA 2024 report (State of DevOps)," https://dora.dev/research/2024/dora-report/
67

The only metric that matters to them is: Did the code pass the test? But the projects used for the benchmark have incomplete test cases. The generated code might fix the original issue but introduce a new bug. Worse, the code isn't examined to see if it is readable or fits the established patterns of the code base.
- Much of what we're seeing to support the value of GenAI tool is self-report data. As the above research study illustrates, the self-report data doesn't necessarily correspond to reality! As an example, I perceived my last bike ride was 20% faster than the previous one, but the data sadly shows it was merely average.
- DORA report (State of DevOps) - The DORA 2024 report[^5] has missed the boat, measuring developers' perceptions about AI. It found that they feel more productive and believe they have reduced complexity. But, as seen above, self-report data isn't the most reliable when it comes to performance.

More caveats on the research paper:
- There is a risk that the paper's methodology missed something important about real work (although this paper already has a better methodology than previous papers).
- Many of the developers hadn't used Cursor before. Maybe with more practice they would have been faster.
- The study used senior developers. Maybe junior developers would gain more benefit from AI assistance. But then that leaves the question of how do junior developers grow and become senior? Will junior developers spend enough time reviewing the generated code, understand it, and verify that it's a good fit?
- This is a single paper. Maybe a larger sample size or a diffent mix of people might have found a different result.

**What this paper does is give me pause in accepting the statements that claim AI is magically improving developer productivity.** For a concrete example of how AI coding tools struggle with real tasks, see the results of our [AI Code Generation and the Tennis Kata](/blog/ai-code-generation-and-the-tennis-kata/) experiment.
<Figure
  src={aiPromiseReality}
  alt="sketch of GenAI promises vs reality"
  caption="sketch of GenAI promises vs reality"
/>
What would I like to see? I would like papers to look at additional questions not covered in this study:
- Was the code change a sensible size? Generally, we don't want bug fixes to be large changes. When bug fixes are large, it introduces new risks.
- Did the AI generated code fit the idioms used in the project?
- Was the AI generated code readable?
- Did the AI avoid adding any new dependencies?

It is early days in our use of GenAI and software development. The models themselves will likely improve (example: context windows), and tool vendors will find ways to improve their tools so the LLM has more information about the codebase. I also know of some developers who are using a BDD style of development coupled with code generation, which might well pay off.

I hope we all learn to be more skeptical of promises about productivity increases without first examining the methodology underneath. (I, for one, have written off the DORA Reports as unreliable.) In our [Certified ScrumMaster workshops](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/), we focus on what actually helps teams deliver value, not promises of faster output.

<LinkList heading = "Related Blog Entries">
- [AI-Generated Code Quality and the Challenges we all face](/blog/ai-generated-code-quality-problems/)
- [GenAI Code Quality: The Fundamental Flaws and How Bluffing Makes It Worse](/blog/genai-code-quality-fundamental-flaws-and-how-bluffing-makes-it-worse/)
- [GenAI vs Human Intelligence: A Reality Check](/blog/gen-ai-vs-human-intelligence-a-reality-check/)
</LinkList>

[^1]: "The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot," https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590
[^2]: "Significant Productivity Gains through Programming with Large Language Models," https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3661145
[^3]: "Sea Change in Software Development: Economic and Productivity Analysis of the AI-Powered Developer Lifecycle," https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15033
[^4]: "The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers," https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4945566
[^5]: "DORA 2024 report (State of DevOps)," https://dora.dev/research/2024/dora-report/
